Atropisomers in InChI

Some biaryls cannot rotate about the bond between their rings. Their two twisted forms are mirror images that can be separated in a bottle. Standard InChI gives both the same identifier. The new InChI tells them apart.

2,2'-Dibromo-6,6'-dichlorobiphenyl. Standard InChI has no stereo layer for either form: both are InChI=1S/C12H6Br2Cl2/c13-7-3-1-5-9(15)11(7)12-8(14)4-2-6-10(12)16/h1-6H.

What an atropisomer is

Two flat rings joined by a single bond normally spin freely. Bulky groups next to that bond, in the ortho positions, collide when the rings try to pass each other. The molecule stays twisted one way or the other. The bond becomes a chirality axis, like the axis of an allene.

The two forms are named M and P (minus and plus, the sense of the twist), or aR and aS by CIP rules (M = aR, P = aS). InChI writes neither name: it records the twist as a sign in /t and the mirror image in /m, as for any stereocentre.

Whether rotation is slow enough to isolate the forms is chemistry, not something InChI computes. InChI decides from the structure alone, with the rules below.

From drawing to InChI, step by step

Example: the M form above.

  1. You draw the twist

    A wedge on a ring bond at the axis shows which edge of that ring points toward you. Two wedges (one per ring) are usual. One wedge is enough, and 3D coordinates work without any wedge.

    Atropisomers are detected only with the option -EnhancedStereochemistry. Without it, the output is exactly the standard InChI.

  2. InChI looks for an axis

    A bond is a candidate when all of these hold:

    • It is a single bond between two carbons.
    • Each carbon has three non-hydrogen neighbours and no H (a flat, aryl-like end).
    • The bond is not in a ring of 6 atoms or fewer.

    axis   the four ortho positions

  3. InChI checks that rotation is blocked

    At least three of the four ortho positions must carry something other than H. A fused ring counts. When the axis sits inside a ring of exactly 8 atoms, the two bridge positions are enough.

  4. InChI checks that each end is unsymmetric

    The two ortho groups on each ring must differ. If one ring has the same group on both sides, turning it over gives the same molecule: there is no mirror-image pair.

    Here one ring has Cl on both sides. Fully hindered, but not chiral: no axis.

  5. InChI reads the twist

    From the wedges (or the 3D coordinates) InChI computes a parity for the axis, by the same method it uses for allenes. If the drawing is flat, the twist is unknown and the axis is left out, with the warning:

    Warning (Omitted undefined stereo)

  6. InChI writes the axis once

    The two axis carbons get canonical numbers 11 and 12. The axis appears once in /t, on the lower-numbered carbon. Citing both would read like two stereocentres.

    InChI=1B/C12H6Br2Cl2/c13-7-3-1-5-9(15)11(7)12-8(14)4-2-6-10(12)16/h1-6H/t11-/m0/s1
    /t11-
    an axis on carbons 11–12; with one stereo element the sign is always −
    /m0
    which mirror image: /m0 is M, /m1 is P
    /s1
    absolute configuration, as in standard InChI

  7. Check: draw it with one wedge

    Remove the second wedge. The twist is still defined, and the InChI is identical:

    /t11-/m0/s1

Rules at a glance

Carbon–carbon single bonds only

Both ends flat, three-connected, without H. C–N, N–N and C–O axes are not detected yet.

Not in a small ring

A bond in a ring of 6 atoms or fewer is never an axis.

Three of four ortho positions

Substituted, or part of a fused ring. Two are enough inside an 8-membered ring.

Each end unsymmetric

Two equal ortho groups on one ring: no axis.

One wedge, two wedges or 3D

All give the same InChI. A flat drawing gives no axis and a warning.

Written once, in /t

On the lower-numbered axis carbon. The mirror image is in /m.

/t11-/m0/s1

M is /m0, P is /m1

For every M/P-labelled molecule in the test set, 2D and 3D alike.

Prefix 1B

Marks the string as enhanced (beta), never mistaken for a standard InChI.

or and & labels on an axis

The labels of enhanced stereochemistry work on an axis as on a stereocentre: &1 for both forms mixed (racemic), or1 for one form, unknown which.

&1 on the axis: racemic. No /m.

/t11-/s3

or1 instead: /t11-/s2

The label must sit on the lower-numbered axis carbon

Here or1 sits on carbon 12. InChI does not see it and writes the drawn form as absolute, without a warning:

/t11-/m0/s1

What is not detected

In each case the new InChI equals the standard one.

Limits of this version

  • Only carbon–carbon axes. Anilides, N-aryl amides and similar C–N axes are not yet covered.
  • InChI cannot yet turn the axis in /t back into a structure (InChI to molfile).
  • The hindrance rule counts groups; it does not know rotation barriers. Some real atropisomers with only two ortho groups are missed.

Every InChI on this page is computed by the prototype (branch atropisomers, option -EnhancedStereochemistry), not typed in. Full rules: specification Atropisomers. More examples, old vs. new: comparison table.
